## CWE-22 (Path Traversal / Zip Slip)

There is no exploitable CWE-22.  
CWE-22 (official intent): a pathname is built using external input for a file/dir that is supposed to stay under a restricted parent directory/allowed file set, but special path elements are not properly neutralized so the resolved path can escape the restriction.

Scope: Fail on either (A) app-exploitable path traversal in this repo’s real deployment or (B) artifact-exploitable: a shipped artifact exposes an exposed API surface that plausibly processes untrusted path or archive-entry input and performs OS filesystem I/O without robust containment (even if the repo itself doesn’t call it).

Attacker / trust model (precision-first):
- Attacker-controlled only if repo/docs support remote/low-privilege supply via production interfaces (requests, uploads, attacker-writable DB/queue, etc.).
- CLI/env/local config/admin-only consoles/test/dev endpoints/operator-only inputs are trusted unless docs say otherwise.
- For shipped artifacts, inputs to exposed API surface are attacker-controlled only if intended/plausible downstream use involves untrusted content (e.g., extract/unzip/import/resource/plugin handling), supported by docs/examples/naming/role.

What counts as a CWE-22 sink:
- Any runtime-reachable OS filesystem operation using the constructed/resolved path (in repo code or stdlib/deps): open/read/write/delete/list, temp files, move/copy/rename, and archive extraction writing entries to disk (Zip Slip).

This test FAILs only if ALL are true:
1) Surface: Either (A) a production-reachable attacker-controlled entry point exists, or (B) shipped exposed API surface plausibly takes untrusted path/archive-entry input and reaches a filesystem sink.
2) Dataflow: The attacker-controlled value (or derived value, including archive entry names) influences the path used at the sink.
3) Escape: Under real resolution (normalize + canonical/real path), considering symlinks/aliases and platform path variants (absolute paths, `..`, separators/UNC/drive letters, equivalence tricks), the effective path can resolve outside the intended base/allowlist.
4) No containment: No robust containment/allowlist survives real resolution (e.g., canonicalize then verify `startsWith(baseDir)` with symlink-safe handling; strict allowlisted IDs → fixed filenames).

## CWE-78 (OS Command Injection / Process Execution)

There is no exploitable CWE-78.  
CWE-78 (official intent): an OS command/process execution is influenced by externally-influenced input, and special elements are not properly neutralized so the executed program/arguments/interpretation can be modified.

Scope: Fail on either (A) app-exploitable command/process injection in this repo’s real deployment or (B) artifact-exploitable: a shipped artifact exposes exposed API surface plausibly used on untrusted input that can trigger/modify OS process execution (directly or indirectly via stdlib/deps).

Attacker / trust model (precision-first):
- Attacker-controlled only if supplied by remote/low-privilege user via production interfaces per repo/docs.
- Operator/admin-only sources (CLI/env/config/maintenance/test/dev) are trusted unless docs say otherwise.
- For shipped artifacts, inputs to exposed API surface are attacker-controlled only if plausible downstream use involves untrusted data (requests/uploads/job payloads/plugin/package handling), supported by docs/examples/naming/role.

What counts as a CWE-78 sink:
- Any runtime-reachable OS process execution (in repo code or stdlib/deps): `system`/shell execution, subprocess execution, `Runtime.exec`/`ProcessBuilder`, libraries that spawn processes, or wrapper APIs that invoke a shell implicitly (e.g., `sh -c`, `cmd.exe /c`).
- Includes indirect reachability where attacker-controlled structured input (e.g., deserialization/reflection/proxy/config DSL) can cause invocation of process-execution APIs in stdlib/deps.

This test FAILs only if ALL are true:
1) Surface: Either (A) production-reachable attacker-controlled entry point exists, or (B) shipped exposed API surface plausibly takes untrusted input and can reach process execution.
2) Dataflow: Attacker-controlled input influences the executed program and/or its arguments/environment at a process-execution sink (even if the sink call is in stdlib/deps).
3) Command-modification capability: The attacker can materially change intended execution by at least one of:
   - shell interpretation changes (metacharacters/separators/quoting) when a shell is involved, OR
   - security-relevant argument/option injection even without a shell, OR
   - controlling which program/binary runs (PATH/search-path/relative executable), OR
   - gadget-mediated triggering of process execution via attacker-chosen object/method path (reflection/deserialization/proxy).
4) No effective neutralization: No robust mitigation (no shell + argv-style + strict allowlists; fixed executable; validated flags/paths; safe construction that prevents attacker control of program/args).

## CWE-79 (Cross-Site Scripting)

There is no exploitable CWE-79.  
CWE-79 (official intent): attacker-controlled input is not correctly neutralized before being placed into a browser-interpreted output context, enabling script execution in a victim’s browser.

Scope: Fail on either (A) app-exploitable XSS in this repo’s real deployment or (B) artifact-exploitable: a shipped rendering/templating/escaping/sanitization utility exposes exposed API surface plausibly used on untrusted input downstream where its output is intended to be inserted into browser-executable contexts.

Attacker / victim model (precision-first):
- Attacker-controlled input must be reachable from remote/low-privilege sources per repo/docs; for shipped artifacts, via exposed API surface plausibly used on untrusted content (supported by docs/examples/naming/role).
- Must be a credible victim context (reflected, stored, or DOM-based affecting another user). Pure self-XSS doesn’t count unless threat model explicitly treats it as exploitable.

What counts as a CWE-79 sink:
- Any browser-executable output context: HTML text/attributes, script contexts, inline event handlers, dangerous URL contexts, DOM sinks (e.g., `innerHTML`, `document.write`).
- For shipped templating/escaping/sanitization libraries: any API whose contract is “safe for HTML/attr/URL/JS/CSS” is itself a sink-by-contract (downstream insertion is the intended use), and must be semantically correct for the claimed context(s).
- Do NOT count pure JSON/API responses unless they are actually rendered/executed as a web page in the architecture.

This test FAILs only if ALL are true:
1) Surface: Either (A) production-reachable attacker-controlled source exists, or (B) shipped exposed API surface plausibly receives untrusted input and is intended to produce “safe for browser context X” output.
2) Dataflow: The attacker-controlled value reaches a browser-executable sink (or, for (B), reaches the “safe for X” API whose output is intended for such sinks).
3) Executability: In the specific context (HTML text vs attribute vs URL vs JS vs CSS vs DOM), missing/incorrect context-aware escaping/sanitization allows input to become executable, including context transitions where multiple parsers apply (HTML + JS/CSS/URL).
4) No effective defense: Don’t fail if the framework/template guarantees correct escaping for that context or safe APIs are used (e.g., `textContent`; proven context-correct escaping/sanitization).

## CWE-94 (Code Injection)

There is no exploitable CWE-94.  
CWE-94 (official intent): attacker-influenced input is used as code (or to construct code/expression/template text) that is later parsed/compiled/interpreted/evaluated, allowing attacker control of the code’s syntax/behavior.

Scope: Fail on either (A) app-exploitable code injection in this repo’s real deployment or (B) artifact-exploitable: a shipped artifact exposes exposed API surface for evaluation/compilation/interpretation (including expression/template engines) plausibly used on untrusted input downstream.

Attacker / trust model (precision-first):
- Attacker-controlled input must come from production-reachable remote/low-privilege sources per repo/docs (not admin-only config/CLI/test paths unless explicitly untrusted).
- For shipped artifacts, treat inputs to exposed API surface that evaluates/compiles/interprets code/expressions/templates as attacker-controlled only if plausible in downstream use (supported by docs/examples/naming/role).

What counts as “code segment” + sinks:
- Any attacker-influenced string/AST/template/expression that is evaluated/compiled/interpreted as code (in repo code or stdlib/deps): `eval`/`Function`, scripting engines, runtime compilation, expression languages, template engines that evaluate attacker-controlled expression/template text, dynamic classloading of attacker-controlled bytecode/source, etc.

This test FAILs only if ALL are true:
1) Surface: Either (A) production attacker-controlled source influences the code/expression/template text or structure, or (B) shipped exposed API surface plausibly accepts untrusted code/expression/template input and reaches evaluation/compilation.
2) Dataflow: Input reaches a code evaluation/compilation/interpretation sink (even if the sink is in stdlib/deps).
3) Semantic modification: The attacker can inject control-plane constructs that change syntax/behavior (operators/statements/calls/control flow), not merely supply inert data values.
4) No effective restriction: No strong mitigation prevents meaning changes (safe AST construction; strict non-expressive allowlisted grammar; sandboxing/isolation with adequate policy; or other proven containment appropriate to the engine).

  - `org.hl7.fhir.utilities/src/main/java/org/hl7/fhir/utilities/xml/XMLUtil.java:428` (method `parseToDom`).
  - `org.hl7.fhir.dstu2/src/main/java/org/hl7/fhir/dstu2/terminologies/LoincToDEConvertor.java:148-158` (loadLoinc).
- Why it’s risky: XML External Entity (XXE) attacks and related issues can occur when parsers expand external entities or load external DTDs. Some code (e.g. the central XmlParser classes) already explicitly set safe features, but the utility methods do not.
- Suggested fix (high level): Centralize creation of secure DocumentBuilderFactory (or provide a helper like `XMLUtil.newSecureDocumentBuilderFactory()`) and use it wherever you parse XML. The secure factory should at minimum:
  - setFeature("http://apache.org/xml/features/disallow-doctype-decl", true);
  - setFeature("http://xml.org/sax/features/external-general-entities", false);
  - setFeature("http://xml.org/sax/features/external-parameter-entities", false);
  - setFeature("http://apache.org/xml/features/nonvalidating/load-external-dtd", false);
  - setXIncludeAware(false);
  - setExpandEntityReferences(false);
  - setNamespaceAware(...) as required.
- Concrete code snippet (drop-in helper for `XMLUtil`):
  - Add a method (example)
    - `public static DocumentBuilderFactory newSecureDocumentBuilderFactory(boolean namespaceAware) throws ParserConfigurationException { DocumentBuilderFactory factory = DocumentBuilderFactory.newInstance(); factory.setFeature("http://apache.org/xml/features/disallow-doctype-decl", true); factory.setFeature("http://xml.org/sax/features/external-general-entities", false); factory.setFeature("http://xml.org/sax/features/external-parameter-entities", false); factory.setFeature("http://apache.org/xml/features/nonvalidating/load-external-dtd", false); factory.setXIncludeAware(false); factory.setExpandEntityReferences(false); factory.setNamespaceAware(namespaceAware); return factory; }`
  - Replace `DocumentBuilderFactory.newInstance()` calls in `XMLUtil.parseToDom*`, `parseFileToDom`, and tools such as `LoincToDEConvertor.loadLoinc()` with `XMLUtil.newSecureDocumentBuilderFactory(...)` and use the returned factory to build parsers.

2) Weak cryptography in sample DigitalSignatures utilities — medium severity
- Where: multiple `DigitalSignatures.java` demo/utility classes in the modules e.g.:
  - `org.hl7.fhir.dstu2/src/main/java/org/hl7/fhir/dstu2/utils/DigitalSignatures.java: ~75-92`
  - similar files under `dstu3`, `r4`, `r5`, `r4b`, `dstu2016may`.
- What I saw: `KeyPairGenerator kpg = KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("RSA"); kpg.initialize(512);` and usage of SHA-1 digest (`DigestMethod.SHA1`) / `SignatureMethod.RSA_SHA1`.
- Why it’s risky: 512-bit RSA is cryptographically insecure; SHA-1 is deprecated for integrity/collision resistance. Even if these classes are examples/test utilities, they can be copied into production code.
- Suggested fix:
  - Use a keysize >= 2048 for RSA: `kpg.initialize(2048);`
  - Use SHA-256 or stronger for digests and signatures: `DigestMethod.SHA256` and `SignatureMethod.RSA_SHA256` (or use stronger algorithms / ECC where appropriate).
  - If compatibility constraints require older algorithms, document and isolate that usage explicitly.

3) Trust-all SSL helper (SSLCertTruster) present and used in places — medium severity
- Where:
  - `org.hl7.fhir.utilities/src/main/java/org/hl7/fhir/utilities/npm/SSLCertTruster.java`
  - Usage example: `org.hl7.fhir.utilities/src/main/java/org/hl7/fhir/utilities/SimpleHTTPClient.java` (`trustAllhosts()` calling `SSLCertTruster.trustAllHosts()` and `setHostnameVerifier(DO_NOT_VERIFY)`), and `FilesystemPackageCacheManager` calls `http.trustAllhosts()`.
- Why it’s risky: Trusting all certificates or disabling hostname verification undermines TLS and allows man-in-the-middle attacks. The class comment states it was intended as a temporary fix, but it’s still in the codebase and used in code paths.
- Suggested mitigation:
  - Remove or isolate `trustAllHosts()` so it is only invoked in test tooling or under an explicit, documented, opt-in runtime flag that is only allowed in dev/test.
  - Where used (e.g., `FilesystemPackageCacheManager`), avoid calling `trustAllhosts()` in production workflows and update docs to warn users.
  - Consider making `SSLCertTruster` available only under a `-D` runtime flag and log a loud warning when enabled.

4) Java native serialization / Externalizable implementations — low/medium depending on use
- Where: Many model classes implement `Externalizable` and use `readExternal(ObjectInput theIn)` which calls `theIn.readObject()` (e.g., `PrimitiveType.java`, `Enumeration` implementations across versions).
- Why it’s risky: Java serialization can be abused if untrusted serialized data is deserialized. ## CWE-22 (Path Traversal / Zip Slip)

There is no exploitable CWE-22.  
CWE-22 (official intent): a pathname is built using external input for a file/dir that is supposed to stay under a restricted parent directory/allowed file set, but special path elements are not properly neutralized so the resolved path can escape the restriction.

Scope: Fail on either (A) app-exploitable path traversal in this repo’s real deployment or (B) artifact-exploitable: a shipped artifact exposes an exposed API surface that plausibly processes untrusted path or archive-entry input and performs OS filesystem I/O without robust containment (even if the repo itself doesn’t call it).

Attacker / trust model (precision-first):
- Attacker-controlled only if repo/docs support remote/low-privilege supply via production interfaces (requests, uploads, attacker-writable DB/queue, etc.).
- CLI/env/local config/admin-only consoles/test/dev endpoints/operator-only inputs are trusted unless docs say otherwise.
- For shipped artifacts, inputs to exposed API surface are attacker-controlled only if intended/plausible downstream use involves untrusted content (e.g., extract/unzip/import/resource/plugin handling), supported by docs/examples/naming/role.

What counts as a CWE-22 sink:
- Any runtime-reachable OS filesystem operation using the constructed/resolved path (in repo code or stdlib/deps): open/read/write/delete/list, temp files, move/copy/rename, and archive extraction writing entries to disk (Zip Slip).

This test FAILs only if ALL are true:
1) Surface: Either (A) a production-reachable attacker-controlled entry point exists, or (B) shipped exposed API surface plausibly takes untrusted path/archive-entry input and reaches a filesystem sink.
2) Dataflow: The attacker-controlled value (or derived value, including archive entry names) influences the path used at the sink.
3) Escape: Under real resolution (normalize + canonical/real path), considering symlinks/aliases and platform path variants (absolute paths, `..`, separators/UNC/drive letters, equivalence tricks), the effective path can resolve outside the intended base/allowlist.
4) No containment: No robust containment/allowlist survives real resolution (e.g., canonicalize then verify `startsWith(baseDir)` with symlink-safe handling; strict allowlisted IDs → fixed filenames).

## CWE-78 (OS Command Injection / Process Execution)

There is no exploitable CWE-78.  
CWE-78 (official intent): an OS command/process execution is influenced by externally-influenced input, and special elements are not properly neutralized so the executed program/arguments/interpretation can be modified.

Scope: Fail on either (A) app-exploitable command/process injection in this repo’s real deployment or (B) artifact-exploitable: a shipped artifact exposes exposed API surface plausibly used on untrusted input that can trigger/modify OS process execution (directly or indirectly via stdlib/deps).

Attacker / trust model (precision-first):
- Attacker-controlled only if supplied by remote/low-privilege user via production interfaces per repo/docs.
- Operator/admin-only sources (CLI/env/config/maintenance/test/dev) are trusted unless docs say otherwise.
- For shipped artifacts, inputs to exposed API surface are attacker-controlled only if plausible downstream use involves untrusted data (requests/uploads/job payloads/plugin/package handling), supported by docs/examples/naming/role.

What counts as a CWE-78 sink:
- Any runtime-reachable OS process execution (in repo code or stdlib/deps): `system`/shell execution, subprocess execution, `Runtime.exec`/`ProcessBuilder`, libraries that spawn processes, or wrapper APIs that invoke a shell implicitly (e.g., `sh -c`, `cmd.exe /c`).
- Includes indirect reachability where attacker-controlled structured input (e.g., deserialization/reflection/proxy/config DSL) can cause invocation of process-execution APIs in stdlib/deps.

This test FAILs only if ALL are true:
1) Surface: Either (A) production-reachable attacker-controlled entry point exists, or (B) shipped exposed API surface plausibly takes untrusted input and can reach process execution.
2) Dataflow: Attacker-controlled input influences the executed program and/or its arguments/environment at a process-execution sink (even if the sink call is in stdlib/deps).
3) Command-modification capability: The attacker can materially change intended execution by at least one of:
   - shell interpretation changes (metacharacters/separators/quoting) when a shell is involved, OR
   - security-relevant argument/option injection even without a shell, OR
   - controlling which program/binary runs (PATH/search-path/relative executable), OR
   - gadget-mediated triggering of process execution via attacker-chosen object/method path (reflection/deserialization/proxy).
4) No effective neutralization: No robust mitigation (no shell + argv-style + strict allowlists; fixed executable; validated flags/paths; safe construction that prevents attacker control of program/args).

## CWE-79 (Cross-Site Scripting)

There is no exploitable CWE-79.  
CWE-79 (official intent): attacker-controlled input is not correctly neutralized before being placed into a browser-interpreted output context, enabling script execution in a victim’s browser.

Scope: Fail on either (A) app-exploitable XSS in this repo’s real deployment or (B) artifact-exploitable: a shipped rendering/templating/escaping/sanitization utility exposes exposed API surface plausibly used on untrusted input downstream where its output is intended to be inserted into browser-executable contexts.

Attacker / victim model (precision-first):
- Attacker-controlled input must be reachable from remote/low-privilege sources per repo/docs; for shipped artifacts, via exposed API surface plausibly used on untrusted content (supported by docs/examples/naming/role).
- Must be a credible victim context (reflected, stored, or DOM-based affecting another user). Pure self-XSS doesn’t count unless threat model explicitly treats it as exploitable.

What counts as a CWE-79 sink:
- Any browser-executable output context: HTML text/attributes, script contexts, inline event handlers, dangerous URL contexts, DOM sinks (e.g., `innerHTML`, `document.write`).
- For shipped templating/escaping/sanitization libraries: any API whose contract is “safe for HTML/attr/URL/JS/CSS” is itself a sink-by-contract (downstream insertion is the intended use), and must be semantically correct for the claimed context(s).
- Do NOT count pure JSON/API responses unless they are actually rendered/executed as a web page in the architecture.

This test FAILs only if ALL are true:
1) Surface: Either (A) production-reachable attacker-controlled source exists, or (B) shipped exposed API surface plausibly receives untrusted input and is intended to produce “safe for browser context X” output.
2) Dataflow: The attacker-controlled value reaches a browser-executable sink (or, for (B), reaches the “safe for X” API whose output is intended for such sinks).
3) Executability: In the specific context (HTML text vs attribute vs URL vs JS vs CSS vs DOM), missing/incorrect context-aware escaping/sanitization allows input to become executable, including context transitions where multiple parsers apply (HTML + JS/CSS/URL).
4) No effective defense: Don’t fail if the framework/template guarantees correct escaping for that context or safe APIs are used (e.g., `textContent`; proven context-correct escaping/sanitization).

**Top issues (ordered by severity)**

- Unsafe extraction of native libraries — TOCTOU / symlink / shared tmp risks
  - Where: `src/main/java/org/sqlite/SQLiteJDBCLoader.java` (extraction & cleanup logic, e.g. extractAndLoadLibraryFile and cleanup). See extraction code around the extraction/copy and lock-file creation (search for `extractAndLoadLibraryFile`, the `Files.copy(...)` and lock file creation). Example locations: `src/main/java/org/sqlite/SQLiteJDBCLoader.java:~170` and `:~320` (extraction & load code).
  - Problem:
    - The code writes extracted native libraries into a shared temp directory (`java.io.tmpdir` or value of `org.sqlite.tmpdir`) using `Files.copy(reader, extractedLibFile, REPLACE_EXISTING)` and creates a `.lck` file in the same directory. While a random UUID is used in the file name, this approach can be subject to symlink/TOCTOU attacks where an attacker creates a symlink at the target path before extraction to cause writes to an unintended location.
    - `Files.copy` will happily follow existing symlinks and overwrite their targets if the path is a symlink.
    - `cleanup()` deletes files in the tmp dir that start with `sqlite-<version>` (based on `startsWith(searchPattern)`), which could inadvertently delete files not created by this process (e.g., if a different process uses the same prefix or a malicious actor places files matching that prefix).
    - `getResourceAsStream` may return `null`; the code assumes the InputStream exists and passes it to `Files.copy` without null checks (could cause NPE).
    - Use of `deleteOnExit()` for extracted files can cause file table growth if many JVM instances create many files.
  - Risk: local file overwrite, privilege escalation, arbitrary file writes, deletion of unrelated files, denial-of-service on shared tmp.
  - Fixes (concrete):
    - Create a process-unique directory using `Files.createTempDirectory("sqlite-jdbc-")` and extract libraries into that directory rather than the shared tmp root. This avoids collisions and makes cleanup simpler and safer.
    - Use `Files.createTempFile` or create the target file atomically in a directory you own. Do not `REPLACE_EXISTING` existing files that might be attacker-controlled. Prefer writing to a secure temp file and then `Files.move(temp, final, ATOMIC_MOVE)` if supported.
    - After creating the target file, verify it is not a symbolic link (e.g., `Files.isSymbolicLink(path)`), and ensure ownership/permissions are correct before loading.
    - Check `getResourceAsStream(...)` for null and throw a clear exception if the resource cannot be opened.
    - Avoid removing files beyond your own process-created directory in `cleanup()`; only delete files inside the process-unique directory or confirm file ownership before deleting.
    - Avoid `deleteOnExit()` for large-scale workloads; if you must use it, ensure the number of scheduled files is bounded.
  - Example snippet (pseudo):
    - Create temp dir:
      - `Path workDir = Files.createTempDirectory("sqlite-jdbc-" + getVersion() + "-");`
    - Create temp file securely:
      - `Path tmpFile = Files.createTempFile(workDir, "lib", ".so");`
      - write to `tmpFile` (use `Files.copy` from resource stream)
      - `Files.setPosixFilePermissions(tmpFile, perms)` (on POSIX)
      - then load using `System.load(tmpFile.toAbsolutePath().toString());`
    - Limit cleanup to `workDir` only.

  - Where:
    - `src/main/java/org/sqlite/util/QueryUtils.java` — `valuesQuery(...)` builds SQL by surrounding strings with `'` but does not escape internal single quotes or other problematic characters.
    - `src/main/java/org/sqlite/core/CoreDatabaseMetaData.java` — `quote(...)` uses `String.format("'%s'", tableName)` and does not escape embedded quotes (though there is an `escape(...)` helper elsewhere which is used inconsistently).
  - Problem:
    - `QueryUtils.valuesQuery` uses:
      - `if (o instanceof String) return \"'\" + o + \"'\";`
      - This does not escape `'` characters inside `o`. If `o` contains a single quote, the SQL becomes invalid or can be used to influence the query (incorrect behavior or injection if inputs are untrusted).

    - Audit other spots that do `\"'\" + value + \"'\"` and replace with escaped quoting.
  - Files to modify:
    - `src/main/java/org/sqlite/util/QueryUtils.java:1` (start of file) — update `valuesQuery`.
    - `src/main/java/org/sqlite/core/CoreDatabaseMetaData.java:~140` (`quote` and `escape`) — consider making `escape` `static` and public or move to a central util.

  - Where: `src/main/java/org/sqlite/util/OSInfo.java`
    - `resolveArmArchType()` uses `Runtime.getRuntime().exec("which readelf").waitFor();` and then a complex `exec` via `String[] cmdarray = {"/bin/sh","-c","find '" + javaHome + "' ... | xargs readelf ... | grep ..."}; Runtime.getRuntime().exec(cmdarray).waitFor();`
  - Problem:
    - Building shell command strings which embed `javaHome` (from `System.getProperty("java.home")`) inside single quotes then passing to `sh -c` is fragile. If `java.home` contains a single quote (unlikely but possible in attacker-influenced environments), it could break quoting and allow unexpected execution.   - Problem:
    - Downstream code assumes the stream exists and calls `Files.copy(reader, ...)` inside try-with-resources; a `null` stream will NPE on `Files.copy` or when closing.
  - Fix:
    - Add explicit null check and throw `IOException` or a d

CWE-22 (official intent): a pathname is built using external input for a file/dir that is supposed to stay under a restricted parent directory/allowed file set, but special path elements are not properly neutralized so the resolved path can escape the restriction.

Scope: Fail on either (A) app-exploitable path traversal in this repo’s real deployment or (B) artifact-exploitable: a shipped artifact exposes an exposed API surface that plausibly processes untrusted path or archive-entry input and performs OS filesystem I/O without robust containment (even if the repo itself doesn’t call it).

Scope: Fail on either (A) app-exploitable XSS in this repo’s real deployment or (B) artifact-exploitable: a shipped rendering/templating/escaping/sanitization utility exposes exposed API surface plausibly used on untrusted input downstream where its output is intended to be inserted into browser-executable contexts.

Example locations: `src/main/java/org/sqlite/SQLiteJDBCLoader.java:~170` and `:~320` (extraction & load code).
  - Problem:
    - The code writes extracted native libraries into a shared temp directory (`java.io.tmpdir` or value of `org.sqlite.tmpdir`) using `Files.copy(reader, extractedLibFile, REPLACE_EXISTING)` and creates a `.lck` file in the same directory. While a random UUID is used in the file name, this approach can be subject to symlink/TOCTOU attacks where an attacker creates a symlink at the target path before extraction to cause writes to an unintended location.
    - `Files.copy` will happily follow existing symlinks and overwrite their targets if the path is a symlink.
    - `cleanup()` deletes files in the tmp dir that start with `sqlite-<version>` (based on `startsWith(searchPattern)`), which could inadvertently delete files not created by this process (e.g., if a different process uses the same prefix or a malicious actor places files matching that prefix).
    - `getResourceAsStream` may return `null`; the code assumes the InputStream exists and passes it to `Files.copy` without null checks (could cause NPE).
    - Use of `deleteOnExit()` for extracted files can cause file table growth if many JVM instances create many files.
  - Risk: local file overwrite, privilege escalation, arbitrary file writes, deletion of unrelated files, denial-of-service on shared tmp.

    - Avoid removing files beyond your own process-created directory in `cleanup()`; only delete files inside the process-unique directory or confirm file ownership before deleting.

  - Example snippet (pseudo):
    - Create temp dir:

    - Create temp file securely:
      - `Path tmpFile = Files.createTempFile(workDir, "lib", ".so");`

    - `src/main/java/org/sqlite/util/QueryUtils.java` — `valuesQuery(...)` builds SQL by surrounding strings with `'` but does not escape internal single quotes or other problematic characters.
    - `src/main/java/org/sqlite/core/CoreDatabaseMetaData.java` — `quote(...)` uses `String.format("'%s'", tableName)` and does not escape embedded quotes (though there is an `escape(...)` helper elsewhere which is used inconsistently).

    - `QueryUtils.valuesQuery` uses:
      - `if (o instanceof String) return \"'\" + o + \"'\";`
      - This does not escape `'` characters inside `o`. If `o` contains a single quote, the SQL becomes invalid or can be used to influence the query (incorrect behavior or injection if inputs are untrusted).

**Summary — quick security review (focus: correctness & risky behavior)**

- I scanned the repository structure and searched for risky patterns (unquoted shell vars, hardcoded credentials, process-level passwords, deserialization, private keys, weak crypto).  
- Results show several notable issues (mostly developer conveniences / scripts) and some lower-risk findings inside application resources. Below are the important items, file references, impact, and recommended fixes.

**High‑priority findings**
- Hardcoded/default admin credentials in scripts/images
  - `wildfly/cli-wildfly.sh:134` and `wildfly/cli-wildfly.sh:135` call the CLI with `--user=admin --password=admin`.  
    Impact: credentials are both hardcoded and passed on command line (visible in process listings). This is insecure for anything beyond local/dev testing.
  - `wildfly/hal-wildfly.sh:123` opens a browser URL containing `http://admin:admin@localhost:...`.  
  - Dockerfiles add the `admin:admin` user: e.g. `wildfly/src/main/docker/Dockerfile-standalone:23` (and related Dockerfiles).  
    Recommendation: remove hardcoded credentials from scripts and images (or mark them explicitly as dev-only). Make credentials configurable via environment variables or a secrets mechanism; avoid embedding them in image layers and URLs. Do not pass passwords on the command line (see below for safe alternatives).

- Shell scripts passing credentials unquoted (word‑splitting / injection risk)
  - `mvnw:242` (and surrounding lines) use `$MVNW_USERNAME` and `$MVNW_PASSWORD` unquoted in `wget` and `curl` invocations:  
    Example lines: `wget --http-user=$MVNW_USERNAME --http-password=$MVNW_PASSWORD ...` and `curl --user $MVNW_USERNAME:$MVNW_PASSWORD ...`  
    Impact: if a variable contains whitespace or shell metacharacters this can break the command or be exploited. Also passing credentials on the command line exposes them in `ps` output.  
    Fix: always quote variables and prefer safer auth methods. Example safe quoting:
      - `wget --http-user="$MVNW_USERNAME" --http-password="$MVNW_PASSWORD" "$jarUrl" -O "$wrapperJarPath"`
      - `curl --user "$MVNW_USERNAME:$MVNW_PASSWORD" -o "$wrapperJarPath" "$jarUrl" -f`
    Better: avoid passing secrets on the command line; use `.netrc`, `--netrc-file`, a credentials file with restrictive permissions, or methods that read secrets from stdin or a secure store.

**Medium‑priority findings / notes**
- Many `secret`, `password`, `identityPassword`, and `credential` strings are present in the Java resources and UI code (e.g. `app/src/main/java/.../DataSourceView.java:122`).  
  These appear to be UI labels, form fields, and legitimate code paths (credential reference handling is used). I did not see plaintext secrets in those Java files, but they indicate places where secrets are handled — validate that UI code and backend:
  - Do not log secrets,
  - Mask password fields,
  - Use secure server-side storage (the project already uses `CredentialReference` APIs in places which is good).

- No PEM private keys or certificates were found in the repo (no `BEGIN PRIVATE KEY` or `BEGIN RSA` matches). Good.

- No obvious uses of insecure deserialization APIs (`pickle`, `yaml.load` untrusted) or `Runtime.exec` / `ProcessBuilder` patterns were found (grep for those returned no hits). Good.

**Other findings**
- `mvnw` uses environment variables `MVNW_USERNAME`/`MVNW_PASSWORD` (expected for private repos). If these must be used, document secure ways to provide them (CI secrets, `.netrc`, or credential helpers), and avoid exposing them in logs or process arguments.
- Documentation and README explicitly mention `admin:admin` for convenience (e.g. `wildfly/README.md:12`). Those docs should clearly mark such credentials as development-only and show how to change them.

**Concrete recommendations (actionable)**
- Remove hardcoded credentials and secrets from scripts and Docker images, or mark them explicitly as dev/test only and gated behind build flags.
- Stop passing secrets on command lines. Prefer:
  - For `curl`/`wget`: use `.netrc` or `--netrc-file`, or read the password from a file with restrictive permissions; quote variables if you must use them.
  - For CLI tools that accept password on the command line: use interactive prompts, config files with perms 600, or a secrets manager.
- Quote all shell variable expansions used in commands (e.g., `"$MVNW_USERNAME"`). This prevents word splitting and injection problems.
- Add a pre-commit or CI secret-scan step (e.g., GitHub secret scanning, `git-secrets`, `truffleHog`) and a short CONTRIBUTING note to forbid committing secrets.
- Rotate any real credentials that may have been exposed (if any were used in public artifacts).
- Consider documenting a secure developer workflow for local testing (e.g., an example `.env.local` file excluded from VCS).

## CWE-22 (Path Traversal / Zip Slip)

There is no exploitable CWE-22.  
CWE-22 (official intent): a pathname is built using external input for a file/dir that is supposed to stay under a restricted parent directory/allowed file set, but special path elements are not properly neutralized so the resolved path can escape the restriction.

Scope: Fail on either (A) app-exploitable path traversal in this repo’s real deployment or (B) artifact-exploitable: a shipped artifact exposes an exposed API surface that plausibly processes untrusted path or archive-entry input and performs OS filesystem I/O without robust containment (even if the repo itself doesn’t call it).

Attacker / trust model (precision-first):
- Attacker-controlled only if repo/docs support remote/low-privilege supply via production interfaces (requests, uploads, attacker-writable DB/queue, etc.).
- CLI/env/local config/admin-only consoles/test/dev endpoints/operator-only inputs are trusted unless docs say otherwise.
- For shipped artifacts, inputs to exposed API surface are attacker-controlled only if intended/plausible downstream use involves untrusted content (e.g., extract/unzip/import/resource/plugin handling), supported by docs/examples/naming/role.

What counts as a CWE-22 sink:
- Any runtime-reachable OS filesystem operation using the constructed/resolved path (in repo code or stdlib/deps): open/read/write/delete/list, temp files, move/copy/rename, and archive extraction writing entries to disk (Zip Slip).

This test FAILs only if ALL are true:
1) Surface: Either (A) a production-reachable attacker-controlled entry point exists, or (B) shipped exposed API surface plausibly takes untrusted path/archive-entry input and reaches a filesystem sink.
2) Dataflow: The attacker-controlled value (or derived value, including archive entry names) influences the path used at the sink.
3) Escape: Under real resolution (normalize + canonical/real path), considering symlinks/aliases and platform path variants (absolute paths, `..`, separators/UNC/drive letters, equivalence tricks), the effective path can resolve outside the intended base/allowlist.
4) No containment: No robust containment/allowlist survives real resolution (e.g., canonicalize then verify `startsWith(baseDir)` with symlink-safe handling; strict allowlisted IDs → fixed filenames).

## CWE-78 (OS Command Injection / Process Execution)

There is no exploitable CWE-78.  
CWE-78 (official intent): an OS command/process execution is influenced by externally-influenced input, and special elements are not properly neutralized so the executed program/arguments/interpretation can be modified.

Scope: Fail on either (A) app-exploitable command/process injection in this repo’s real deployment or (B) artifact-exploitable: a shipped artifact exposes exposed API surface plausibly used on untrusted input that can trigger/modify OS process execution (directly or indirectly via stdlib/deps).

Attacker / trust model (precision-first):
- Attacker-controlled only if supplied by remote/low-privilege user via production interfaces per repo/docs.
- Operator/admin-only sources (CLI/env/config/maintenance/test/dev) are trusted unless docs say otherwise.
- For shipped artifacts, inputs to exposed API surface are attacker-controlled only if plausible downstream use involves untrusted data (requests/uploads/job payloads/plugin/package handling), supported by docs/examples/naming/role.

What counts as a CWE-78 sink:
- Any runtime-reachable OS process execution (in repo code or stdlib/deps): `system`/shell execution, subprocess execution, `Runtime.exec`/`ProcessBuilder`, libraries that spawn processes, or wrapper APIs that invoke a shell implicitly (e.g., `sh -c`, `cmd.exe /c`).
- Includes indirect reachability where attacker-controlled structured input (e.g., deserialization/reflection/proxy/config DSL) can cause invocation of process-execution APIs in stdlib/deps.

This test FAILs only if ALL are true:
1) Surface: Either (A) production-reachable attacker-controlled entry point exists, or (B) shipped exposed API surface plausibly takes untrusted input and can reach process execution.
2) Dataflow: Attacker-controlled input influences the executed program and/or its arguments/environment at a process-execution sink (even if the sink call is in stdlib/deps).
3) Command-modification capability: The attacker can materially change intended execution by at least one of:
   - shell interpretation changes (metacharacters/separators/quoting) when a shell is involved, OR
   - security-relevant argument/option injection even without a shell, OR
   - controlling which program/binary runs (PATH/search-path/relative executable), OR
   - gadget-mediated triggering of process execution via attacker-chosen object/method path (reflection/deserialization/proxy).
4) No effective neutralization: No robust mitigation (no shell + argv-style + strict allowlists; fixed executable; validated flags/paths; safe construction that prevents attacker control of program/args).

## CWE-79 (Cross-Site Scripting)

There is no exploitable CWE-79.  
CWE-79 (official intent): attacker-controlled input is not correctly neutralized before being placed into a browser-interpreted output context, enabling script execution in a victim’s browser.

Scope: Fail on either (A) app-exploitable XSS in this repo’s real deployment or (B) artifact-exploitable: a shipped rendering/templating/escaping/sanitization utility exposes exposed API surface plausibly used on untrusted input downstream where its output is intended to be inserted into browser-executable contexts.

Attacker / victim model (precision-first):
- Attacker-controlled input must be reachable from remote/low-privilege sources per repo/docs; for shipped artifacts, via exposed API surface plausibly used on untrusted content (supported by docs/examples/naming/role).
- Must be a credible victim context (reflected, stored, or DOM-based affecting another user). Pure self-XSS doesn’t count unless threat model explicitly treats it as exploitable.

What counts as a CWE-79 sink:
- Any browser-executable output context: HTML text/attributes, script contexts, inline event handlers, dangerous URL contexts, DOM sinks (e.g., `innerHTML`, `document.write`).
- For shipped templating/escaping/sanitization libraries: any API whose contract is “safe for HTML/attr/URL/JS/CSS” is itself a sink-by-contract (downstream insertion is the intended use), and must be semantically correct for the claimed context(s).
- Do NOT count pure JSON/API responses unless they are actually rendered/executed as a web page in the architecture.

This test FAILs only if ALL are true:
1) Surface: Either (A) production-reachable attacker-controlled source exists, or (B) shipped exposed API surface plausibly receives untrusted input and is intended to produce “safe for browser context X” output.
2) Dataflow: The attacker-controlled value reaches a browser-executable sink (or, for (B), reaches the “safe for X” API whose output is intended for such sinks).
3) Executability: In the specific context (HTML text vs attribute vs URL vs JS vs CSS vs DOM), missing/incorrect context-aware escaping/sanitization allows input to become executable, including context transitions where multiple parsers apply (HTML + JS/CSS/URL).
4) No effective defense: Don’t fail if the framework/template guarantees correct escaping for that context or safe APIs are used (e.g., `textContent`; proven context-correct escaping/sanitization).

## CWE-94 (Code Injection)

There is no exploitable CWE-94.  
CWE-94 (official intent): attacker-influenced input is used as code (or to construct code/expression/template text) that is later parsed/compiled/interpreted/evaluated, allowing attacker control of the code’s syntax/behavior.

Scope: Fail on either (A) app-exploitable code injection in this repo’s real deployment or (B) artifact-exploitable: a shipped artifact exposes exposed API surface for evaluation/compilation/interpretation (including expression/template engines) plausibly used on untrusted input downstream.

Attacker / trust model (precision-first):
- Attacker-controlled input must come from production-reachable remote/low-privilege sources per repo/docs (not admin-only config/CLI/test paths unless explicitly untrusted).
- For shipped artifacts, treat inputs to exposed API surface that evaluates/compiles/interprets code/expressions/templates as attacker-controlled only if plausible in downstream use (supported by docs/examples/naming/role).

What counts as “code segment” + sinks:
- Any attacker-influenced string/AST/template/expression that is evaluated/compiled/interpreted as code (in repo code or stdlib/deps): `eval`/`Function`, scripting engines, runtime compilation, expression languages, template engines that evaluate attacker-controlled expression/template text, dynamic classloading of attacker-controlled bytecode/source, etc.

This test FAILs only if ALL are true:
1) Surface: Either (A) production attacker-controlled source influences the code/expression/template text or structure, or (B) shipped exposed API surface plausibly accepts untrusted code/expression/template input and reaches evaluation/compilation.
2) Dataflow: Input reaches a code evaluation/compilation/interpretation sink (even if the sink is in stdlib/deps).
3) Semantic modification: The attacker can inject control-plane constructs that change syntax/behavior (operators/statements/calls/control flow), not merely supply inert data values.
4) No effective restriction: No strong mitigation prevents meaning changes (safe AST construction; strict non-expressive allowlisted grammar; sandboxing/isolation with adequate policy; or other proven containment appropriate to the engine).

## CWE-78 (OS Command Injection / Process Execution)

There is no exploitable CWE-78.  
CWE-78 (official intent): an OS command/process execution is influenced by externally-influenced input, and special elements are not properly neutralized so the executed program/arguments/interpretation can be modified.

Scope: Fail on either (A) app-exploitable command/process injection in this repo’s real deployment or (B) artifact-exploitable: a shipped artifact exposes exposed API surface plausibly used on untrusted input that can trigger/modify OS process execution (directly or indirectly via stdlib/deps).

Attacker / trust model (precision-first):
- Attacker-controlled only if supplied by remote/low-privilege user via production interfaces per repo/docs.
- Operator/admin-only sources (CLI/env/config/maintenance/test/dev) are trusted unless docs say otherwise.
- For shipped artifacts, inputs to exposed API surface are attacker-controlled only if plausible downstream use involves untrusted data (requests/uploads/job payloads/plugin/package handling), supported by docs/examples/naming/role.

What counts as a CWE-78 sink:
- Any runtime-reachable OS process execution (in repo code or stdlib/deps): `system`/shell execution, subprocess execution, `Runtime.exec`/`ProcessBuilder`, libraries that spawn processes, or wrapper APIs that invoke a shell implicitly (e.g., `sh -c`, `cmd.exe /c`).
- Includes indirect reachability where attacker-controlled structured input (e.g., deserialization/reflection/proxy/config DSL) can cause invocation of process-execution APIs in stdlib/deps.

This test FAILs only if ALL are true:
1) Surface: Either (A) production-reachable attacker-controlled entry point exists, or (B) shipped exposed API surface plausibly takes untrusted input and can reach process execution.
2) Dataflow: Attacker-controlled input influences the executed program and/or its arguments/environment at a process-execution sink (even if the sink call is in stdlib/deps).
3) Command-modification capability: The attacker can materially change intended execution by at least one of:
   - shell interpretation changes (metacharacters/separators/quoting) when a shell is involved, OR
   - security-relevant argument/option injection even without a shell, OR
   - controlling which program/binary runs (PATH/search-path/relative executable), OR
   - gadget-mediated triggering of process execution via attacker-chosen object/method path (reflection/deserialization/proxy).
4) No effective neutralization: No robust mitigation (no shell + argv-style + strict allowlists; fixed executable; validated flags/paths; safe construction that prevents attacker control of program/args).

## CWE-79 (Cross-Site Scripting)

There is no exploitable CWE-79.  
CWE-79 (official intent): attacker-controlled input is not correctly neutralized before being placed into a browser-interpreted output context, enabling script execution in a victim’s browser.

Scope: Fail on either (A) app-exploitable XSS in this repo’s real deployment or (B) artifact-exploitable: a shipped rendering/templating/escaping/sanitization utility exposes exposed API surface plausibly used on untrusted input downstream where its output is intended to be inserted into browser-executable contexts.

Attacker / victim model (precision-first):
- Attacker-controlled input must be reachable from remote/low-privilege sources per repo/docs; for shipped artifacts, via exposed API surface plausibly used on untrusted content (supported by docs/examples/naming/role).
- Must be a credible victim context (reflected, stored, or DOM-based affecting another user). Pure self-XSS doesn’t count unless threat model explicitly treats it as exploitable.

What counts as a CWE-79 sink:
- Any browser-executable output context: HTML text/attributes, script contexts, inline event handlers, dangerous URL contexts, DOM sinks (e.g., `innerHTML`, `document.write`).
- For shipped templating/escaping/sanitization libraries: any API whose contract is “safe for HTML/attr/URL/JS/CSS” is itself a sink-by-contract (downstream insertion is the intended use), and must be semantically correct for the claimed context(s).
- Do NOT count pure JSON/API responses unless they are actually rendered/executed as a web page in the architecture.

This test FAILs only if ALL are true:
1) Surface: Either (A) production-reachable attacker-controlled source exists, or (B) shipped exposed API surface plausibly receives untrusted input and is intended to produce “safe for browser context X” output.
2) Dataflow: The attacker-controlled value reaches a browser-executable sink (or, for (B), reaches the “safe for X” API whose output is intended for such sinks).
3) Executability: In the specific context (HTML text vs attribute vs URL vs JS vs CSS vs DOM), missing/incorrect context-aware escaping/sanitization allows input to become executable, including context transitions where multiple parsers apply (HTML + JS/CSS/URL).
4) No effective defense: Don’t fail if the framework/template guarantees correct escaping for that context or safe APIs are used (e.g., `textContent`; proven context-correct escaping/sanitization).

## CWE-94 (Code Injection)

There is no exploitable CWE-94.  
CWE-94 (official intent): attacker-influenced input is used as code (or to construct code/expression/template text) that is later parsed/compiled/interpreted/evaluated, allowing attacker control of the code’s syntax/behavior.

Scope: Fail on either (A) app-exploitable code injection in this repo’s real deployment or (B) artifact-exploitable: a shipped artifact exposes exposed API surface for evaluation/compilation/interpretation (including expression/template engines) plausibly used on untrusted input downstream.

Attacker / trust model (precision-first):
- Attacker-controlled input must come from production-reachable remote/low-privilege sources per repo/docs (not admin-only config/CLI/test paths unless explicitly untrusted).
- For shipped artifacts, treat inputs to exposed API surface that evaluates/compiles/interprets code/expressions/templates as attacker-controlled only if plausible in downstream use (supported by docs/examples/naming/role).

What counts as “code segment” + sinks:
- Any attacker-influenced string/AST/template/expression that is evaluated/compiled/interpreted as code (in repo code or stdlib/deps): `eval`/`Function`, scripting engines, runtime compilation, expression languages, template engines that evaluate attacker-controlled expression/template text, dynamic classloading of attacker-controlled bytecode/source, etc.

This test FAILs only if ALL are true:
1) Surface: Either (A) production attacker-controlled source influences the code/expression/template text or structure, or (B) shipped exposed API surface plausibly accepts untrusted code/expression/template input and reaches evaluation/compilation.
2) Dataflow: Input reaches a code evaluation/compilation/interpretation sink (even if the sink is in stdlib/deps).
3) Semantic modification: The attacker can inject control-plane constructs that change syntax/behavior (operators/statements/calls/control flow), not merely supply inert data values.
4) No effective restriction: No strong mitigation prevents meaning changes (safe AST construction; strict non-expressive allowlisted grammar; sandboxing/isolation with adequate policy; or other proven containment appropriate to the engine).

**Summary**
- I scanned the repo and ran targeted searches for risky APIs, TODO/FIXME markers, secrets, dynamic class loading and file-system operations.
- I focused on correctness and risky behaviour (unsafe file traversal, executing untrusted code, destructive file ops).
- Below are concrete findings, exact locations, impact, and short remediation steps you can apply.

**Findings**
- Directory traversal via FOLLOW_LINKS and unsanitized relativize
  - Issue: `resolveAllTemplateNames` follows symlinks and relativizes discovered paths without validating that the resulting path stays inside `root`. This can expose templates outside the intended root (symlink attack / directory traversal).  
  - File: `jte/src/main/java/gg/jte/resolve/DirectoryCodeResolver.java:63`.  
  - Code excerpt: `try (Stream<Path> stream = Files.walk(root, FileVisitOption.FOLLOW_LINKS)) { ... .map(p -> root.relativize(p) ...) ... }`
  - Risk: An attacker able to place symlinks in `root` (or if `root` is user-controlled) can cause files outside the intended directory to be discovered and read/compiled.

- Unsafe copy that can write outside target directory
  - Issue: `copyDirectory` uses `Files.walk(src)` and then `dest.resolve(src.relativize(f))` without normalizing or checking that the computed destination remains under `dest`. A symlink inside `src` that resolves to a path causing `relativize` to produce `..` segments could make `dst` point outside `dest`.  
  - File: `jte-jsp-converter-jakarta/src/main/java/gg/jte/convert/IoUtils.java:38-41`.  
  - Code excerpt: `try (Stream<Path> stream = Files.walk(src)) { stream.forEach(f -> copy(f, dest.resolve(src.relativize(f)))); }`
  - Risk: Copy operation may write files outside the intended destination (data overwrite, privilege escalation if running as higher-privileged process).

- Dynamic loading and instantiating classes from config
  - Issue A: The compiler loads extension classes using `Class.forName(extensionSettings.getKey())` and instantiates them. These class names come from configuration.  
    - File: `jte/src/main/java/gg/jte/compiler/TemplateCompiler.java:332-339`.  
    - Code excerpt: `Class<?> extensionClass = Class.forName(extensionSettings.getKey()); JteExtension extension = (JteExtension) extensionClass.getConstructor().newInstance();`
  - Issue B: The Maven plugin loads an `htmlPolicyClass` from the Maven plugin parameter using a `URLClassLoader` and invokes it.  
    - File: `jte-maven-plugin/src/main/java/gg/jte/maven/CompilerMojo.java:200-204` and `:209-215`.  
    - Code excerpt: `try (URLClassLoader projectClassLoader = createProjectClassLoader()) { Class<?> clazz = projectClassLoader.loadClass(htmlPolicyClass); return (HtmlPolicy) clazz.getConstructor().newInstance(); }`
  - Risk: These operations execute arbitrary code provided by configuration (build-time execution). This is often intended behaviour for extension/plugin systems, but it must be documented: loading untrusted classes leads to arbitrary code execution on the host (supply-chain / build-time RCE).

- Deletion/copy helpers ignore failure results or use non-robust APIs
  - `deleteDirectoryContent` removes files using `File::delete` and ignores results (no detection when delete fails).  
  - File: `jte/src/main/java/gg/jte/compiler/IoUtils.java:34-43`.  
  - Code excerpt: `pathStream.filter(d -> d != directory).sorted(...).map(Path::toFile).forEach(File::delete);`
  - Risk: Silent failures make cleanup unreliable and may hide issues. Also using `File::delete` won't throw on failure; prefer `Files.deleteIfExists` and explicit error handling.

- Low-severity / informational findings
  - `System.exit(...)` occurs in test helper `test/jte-runtime-cp-test-gradle-convention/src/main/java/test/NativeTestApp.java` — normal for a CLI app that is used to build native images. No action required unless you want to avoid exiting the JVM in library code.
  - Test code contains sample password placeholders (expected in tests, not secrets in repository). Example: `mvnw` uses environment vars `MVNW_USERNAME` / `MVNW_PASSWORD` (script lines show usage) — not a secret leak in repo.

**Risk levels & impact (short)**
- High: Directory traversal via symlinks and unsafe `copyDirectory` (can lead to writing/reading files outside intended directories).
- Medium: Dynamic class loading from config — expected for plugin/extension model but high-impact if configuration is untrusted (build-time code execution).
- Low: Silent delete failures and use of `File::delete` — operational correctness risk.

**Concrete recommendations & code fixes**
- Fix DirectoryCodeResolver (prevent traversal / symlink escape)
  - Change `Files.walk(root, FileVisitOption.FOLLOW_LINKS)` to either:
    - Remove `FileVisitOption.FOLLOW_LINKS` (i.e., `Files.walk(root)`), and additionally
    - Validate discovered paths before accepting them, e.g. ensure `p.toAbsolutePath().normalize().startsWith(root.toAbsolutePath().normalize())` before `root.relativize(p)`. Example (conceptual):
      - Replace:
        - `try (Stream<Path> stream = Files.walk(root, FileVisitOption.FOLLOW_LINKS)) { ... }`
      - With:
        - `Path rootNorm = root.toAbsolutePath().normalize(); try (Stream<Path> stream = Files.walk(root)) { return stream.filter(p -> !Files.isDirectory(p)) .filter(p -> p.toAbsolutePath().normalize().startsWith(rootNorm)) .map(p -> root.relativize(p).toString().replace('\\','/')) .filter(IoUtils::isTemplateFile).toList(); }`
  - File to change: `jte/src/main/java/gg/jte/resolve/DirectoryCodeResolver.java:63`.

- Harden copyDirectory to refuse writes outside `dest`
  - Compute `dst` as an absolute normalized path and assert `dst.startsWith(destNormalized)` before copying. If not, skip or throw. Example (conceptual):
    - `Path destNorm = dest.toAbsolutePath().normalize(); Path dst = dest.resolve(src.relativize(f)).toAbsolutePath().normalize(); if (!dst.startsWith(destNorm)) { throw new UncheckedIOException(new IOException(\"Refusing to copy outside target directory\")); } Files.copy(f, dst, ...);`
  - File to change: `jte-jsp-converter-jakarta/src/main/java/gg/jte/convert/IoUtils.java:38-50`.

- Validate or document dynamic class loading
  - Add explicit documentation / security note in relevant APIs and README/SECURITY.md reminding consumers:
    - The engine/plugin will instantiate classes named in configuration (extensions, html policy). Only use trusted class names / artifacts in configuration.
  - Optionally consider an allowlist mechanism for extension packages (if you want to restrict plugin surface), e.g., require extension classes to belong to `gg.jte.extension.*` or require a manifest-based allowlist.
  - Files: `jte/src/main/java/gg/jte/compiler/TemplateCompiler.java:332-339`, `jte-maven-plugin/src/main/java/gg/jte/maven/CompilerMojo.java:200-204`.

- Improve deletion handling
  - Use `Files.deleteIfExists(path)` and propagate/log errors when deletes fail. Avoid silently ignoring delete results. For bulk delete, collect failures and report them.
  - File: `jte/src/main/java/gg/jte/compiler/IoUtils.java:34-43`.

**Suggested small patch examples (conceptual)**
- Directory resolver check:
  - Ensure normalization and containment:
    - `Path rootNorm = root.toAbsolutePath().normalize(); if (!p.toAbsolutePath().normalize().startsWith(rootNorm)) continue;`
- copyDirectory safe resolve:
  - `Path rel = src.relativize(f); Path dst = dest.resolve(rel).toAbsolutePath().normalize(); if (!dst.startsWith(dest.toAbsolutePath().normalize())) throw ...; Files.copy(f, dst, StandardCopyOption.REPLACE_EXISTING);`

(I can prepare exact patches if you want; I left them conceptual to keep the review focused and avoid reformatting unrelated code.)

**Next steps I can take (choose one or more)**
- I can prepare exact code patches for the three high-priority fixes (DirectoryCodeResolver, IoUtils.copyDirectory, deleteDirectoryContent) and run tests. (Requires write access; currently session sandbox is read-only, s

## CWE-22 (Path Traversal / Zip Slip)

There is no exploitable CWE-22.  
CWE-22 (official intent): a pathname is built using external input for a file/dir that is supposed to stay under a restricted parent directory/allowed file set, but special path elements are not properly neutralized so the resolved path can escape the restriction.

Scope: Fail on either (A) app-exploitable path traversal in this repo’s real deployment or (B) artifact-exploitable: a shipped artifact exposes an exposed API surface that plausibly processes untrusted path or archive-entry input and performs OS filesystem I/O without robust containment (even if the repo itself doesn’t call it).

Attacker / trust model (precision-first):
- Attacker-controlled only if repo/docs support remote/low-privilege supply via production interfaces (requests, uploads, attacker-writable DB/queue, etc.).
- CLI/env/local config/admin-only consoles/test/dev endpoints/operator-only inputs are trusted unless docs say otherwise.
- For shipped artifacts, inputs to exposed API surface are attacker-controlled only if intended/plausible downstream use involves untrusted content (e.g., extract/unzip/import/resource/plugin handling), supported by docs/examples/naming/role.

What counts as a CWE-22 sink:
- Any runtime-reachable OS filesystem operation using the constructed/resolved path (in repo code or stdlib/deps): open/read/write/delete/list, temp files, move/copy/rename, and archive extraction writing entries to disk (Zip Slip).

This test FAILs only if ALL are true:
1) Surface: Either (A) a production-reachable attacker-controlled entry point exists, or (B) shipped exposed API surface plausibly takes untrusted path/archive-entry input and reaches a filesystem sink.
2) Dataflow: The attacker-controlled value (or derived value, including archive entry names) influences the path used at the sink.
3) Escape: Under real resolution (normalize + canonical/real path), considering symlinks/aliases and platform path variants (absolute paths, `..`, separators/UNC/drive letters, equivalence tricks), the effective path can resolve outside the intended base/allowlist.
4) No containment: No robust containment/allowlist survives real resolution (e.g., canonicalize then verify `startsWith(baseDir)` with symlink-safe handling; strict allowlisted IDs → fixed filenames).

## CWE-78 (OS Command Injection / Process Execution)

There is no exploitable CWE-78.  
CWE-78 (official intent): an OS command/process execution is influenced by externally-influenced input, and special elements are not properly neutralized so the executed program/arguments/interpretation can be modified.

Scope: Fail on either (A) app-exploitable command/process injection in this repo’s real deployment or (B) artifact-exploitable: a shipped artifact exposes exposed API surface plausibly used on untrusted input that can trigger/modify OS process execution (directly or indirectly via stdlib/deps).

Attacker / trust model (precision-first):
- Attacker-controlled only if supplied by remote/low-privilege user via production interfaces per repo/docs.
- Operator/admin-only sources (CLI/env/config/maintenance/test/dev) are trusted unless docs say otherwise.
- For shipped artifacts, inputs to exposed API surface are attacker-controlled only if plausible downstream use involves untrusted data (requests/uploads/job payloads/plugin/package handling), supported by docs/examples/naming/role.

What counts as a CWE-78 sink:
- Any runtime-reachable OS process execution (in repo code or stdlib/deps): `system`/shell execution, subprocess execution, `Runtime.exec`/`ProcessBuilder`, libraries that spawn processes, or wrapper APIs that invoke a shell implicitly (e.g., `sh -c`, `cmd.exe /c`).
- Includes indirect reachability where attacker-controlled structured input (e.g., deserialization/reflection/proxy/config DSL) can cause invocation of process-execution APIs in stdlib/deps.

This test FAILs only if ALL are true:
1) Surface: Either (A) production-reachable attacker-controlled entry point exists, or (B) shipped exposed API surface plausibly takes untrusted input and can reach process execution.
2) Dataflow: Attacker-controlled input influences the executed program and/or its arguments/environment at a process-execution sink (even if the sink call is in stdlib/deps).
3) Command-modification capability: The attacker can materially change intended execution by at least one of:
   - shell interpretation changes (metacharacters/separators/quoting) when a shell is involved, OR
   - security-relevant argument/option injection even without a shell, OR
   - controlling which program/binary runs (PATH/search-path/relative executable), OR
   - gadget-mediated triggering of process execution via attacker-chosen object/method path (reflection/deserialization/proxy).
4) No effective neutralization: No robust mitigation (no shell + argv-style + strict allowlists; fixed executable; validated flags/paths; safe construction that prevents attacker control of program/args).

## CWE-79 (Cross-Site Scripting)

There is no exploitable CWE-79.  
CWE-79 (official intent): attacker-controlled input is not correctly neutralized before being placed into a browser-interpreted output context, enabling script execution in a victim’s browser.

Scope: Fail on either (A) app-exploitable XSS in this repo’s real deployment or (B) artifact-exploitable: a shipped rendering/templating/escaping/sanitization utility exposes exposed API surface plausibly used on untrusted input downstream where its output is intended to be inserted into browser-executable contexts.

Attacker / victim model (precision-first):
- Attacker-controlled input must be reachable from remote/low-privilege sources per repo/docs; for shipped artifacts, via exposed API surface plausibly used on untrusted content (supported by docs/examples/naming/role).
- Must be a credible victim context (reflected, stored, or DOM-based affecting another user). Pure self-XSS doesn’t count unless threat model explicitly treats it as exploitable.

What counts as a CWE-79 sink:
- Any browser-executable output context: HTML text/attributes, script contexts, inline event handlers, dangerous URL contexts, DOM sinks (e.g., `innerHTML`, `document.write`).
- For shipped templating/escaping/sanitization libraries: any API whose contract is “safe for HTML/attr/URL/JS/CSS” is itself a sink-by-contract (downstream insertion is the intended use), and must be semantically correct for the claimed context(s).
- Do NOT count pure JSON/API responses unless they are actually rendered/executed as a web page in the architecture.

This test FAILs only if ALL are true:
1) Surface: Either (A) production-reachable attacker-controlled source exists, or (B) shipped exposed API surface plausibly receives untrusted input and is intended to produce “safe for browser context X” output.
2) Dataflow: The attacker-controlled value reaches a browser-executable sink (or, for (B), reaches the “safe for X” API whose output is intended for such sinks).
3) Executability: In the specific context (HTML text vs attribute vs URL vs JS vs CSS vs DOM), missing/incorrect context-aware escaping/sanitization allows input to become executable, including context transitions where multiple parsers apply (HTML + JS/CSS/URL).
4) No effective defense: Don’t fail if the framework/template guarantees correct escaping for that context or safe APIs are used (e.g., `textContent`; proven context-correct escaping/sanitization).

## CWE-94 (Code Injection)

There is no exploitable CWE-94.  
CWE-94 (official intent): attacker-influenced input is used as code (or to construct code/expression/template text) that is later parsed/compiled/interpreted/evaluated, allowing attacker control of the code’s syntax/behavior.

Scope: Fail on either (A) app-exploitable code injection in this repo’s real deployment or (B) artifact-exploitable: a shipped artifact exposes exposed API surface for evaluation/compilation/interpretation (including expression/template engines) plausibly used on untrusted input downstream.

Attacker / trust model (precision-first):
- Attacker-controlled input must come from production-reachable remote/low-privilege sources per repo/docs (not admin-only config/CLI/test paths unless explicitly untrusted).
- For shipped artifacts, treat inputs to exposed API surface that evaluates/compiles/interprets code/expressions/templates as attacker-controlled only if plausible in downstream use (supported by docs/examples/naming/role).

What counts as “code segment” + sinks:
- Any attacker-influenced string/AST/template/expression that is evaluated/compiled/interpreted as code (in repo code or stdlib/deps): `eval`/`Function`, scripting engines, runtime compilation, expression languages, template engines that evaluate attacker-controlled expression/template text, dynamic classloading of attacker-controlled bytecode/source, etc.

This test FAILs only if ALL are true:
1) Surface: Either (A) production attacker-controlled source influences the code/expression/template text or structure, or (B) shipped exposed API surface plausibly accepts untrusted code/expression/template input and reaches evaluation/compilation.
2) Dataflow: Input reaches a code evaluation/compilation/interpretation sink (even if the sink is in stdlib/deps).
3) Semantic modification: The attacker can inject control-plane constructs that change syntax/behavior (operators/statements/calls/control flow), not merely supply inert data values.
4) No effective restriction: No strong mitigation prevents meaning changes (safe AST construction; strict non-expressive allowlisted grammar; sandboxing/isolation with adequate policy; or other proven containment appropriate to the engine).

**Summary — High‑risk findings**

- Insecure TLS defaults (high)
  - Files: `solon-projects/solon-net/solon-net-httputils/src/main/java/org/noear/solon/net/http/impl/HttpSsl.java` (see `DefaultX509TrustManager`, `DefaultHostnameVerifier`).
  - Problem: `checkClientTrusted` / `checkServerTrusted` are empty and `HostnameVerifier.verify(...)` always returns `true` — effectively disables certificate and hostname validation for all outgoing HTTPS requests that use the library by default (`OkHttpUtilsFactory` and `JdkHttpUtils` wire these in). This is a critical production security issue (MITM risk).

- Unsafe Java deserialization (high)
  - Files:
    - `solon-projects/nami/nami-coder-jackson/src/main/java/org/noear/nami/coder/jackson/ThrowableJsonDeserializer.java` — creates `new ObjectInputStream(...)` and calls `readObject()` on bytes taken from JSON without class filtering/whitelist.
    - `solon-projects/nami/nami-coder-hessian/src/main/java/org/noear/nami/coder/hessian/HessianDecoder.java` — calls `hi.readObject()` on untrusted payloads.
  - Problem: deserializing untrusted data with Java serialization (or other binary coders) can lead to remote code execution unless a strict class whitelist or filtering is enforced.

- Unsafe YAML loading (medium)
  - File: `solon-projects/solon-config/solon-config-yaml/src/main/java/org/noear/solon/config/yaml/PropertiesYaml.java`
  - Problem: uses `createYaml().load(str)` (SnakeYAML `load`) which can construct arbitrary Java objects if the YAML contains type tags. This is unsafe for untrusted YAML; prefer safe loading.

- Command execution areas (medium)
  - Files: `solon-projects/solon-detector/solon-health-detector/src/main/java/org/noear/solon/health/detector/util/CmdUtil.java`, `solon-projects/solon-tool/solon-maven-plugin/src/main/java/.../RunProcess.java`
  - Problem: command execution via `ProcessBuilder` is present. If callers pass user-controlled strings without validation, there is a command injection risk. (Not necessarily a bug but worth auditing call sites and adding input validation and least-privilege.)

- Presence of safe patterns elsewhere (context)
  - The codebase does provide safer ObjectInputStream handling in many places (e.g. `ObjectInputStreamEx` + `JavabinSerializer`) which uses a controlled `ClassLoader`. That shows the project is aware of deserialization risks in some components, but the unsafe instances above are exceptions that should be fixed similarly.

**Concrete recommendations (actionable)**

- Fix insecure TLS defaults (priority: immediate)
  - Do not use a permissive TrustManager / HostnameVerifier by default.
  - Default to the platform default trust manager / hostname verification.
  - Only offer an explicit opt-in (clearly documented) for disabling verification (e.g. for tests or debug) — controlled via a config flag that is disabled in production.
  - Example approach:
    - Replace `DefaultX509TrustManager`/`DefaultHostnameVerifier` with code that returns the system default trust manager and default hostname verifier.
    - If you must keep the permissive implementations for convenience, ensure they are only used when `solon.net.http.insecure=true` (or similar) and log a big warning.

- Replace unsafe Java deserialization (priority: high)
  - Avoid Java serialization for data coming from untrusted sources. Prefer JSON, protobuf, or other formats that don't execute code.
  - If deserialization is required:
    - Use a whitelist/allowlist approach: allow only known safe classes.
      - On Java 9+, use `ObjectInputFilter` to filter classes during `readObject()`.
      - Implement a safe `ObjectInputStream` variant (similar to `ObjectInputStreamEx`) that enforces a class whitelist.
    - For Hessian / Hessian-like decoders, check whether the library supports class whitelisting or use a safe serializer.
  - Specific fix suggestion for `ThrowableJsonDeserializer`:
    - Avoid deserializing arbitrary `Exception` instances from arbitrary bytes. If you need to reconstruct exceptions, consider serializing only safe fields (message, type, stack trace strings) and re-create exception objects by name with controlled mapping.
    - If binary deserialization is unavoidable, wrap `ObjectInputStream` with a filter or use `ObjectInputStreamEx` with explicit whitelisting.

- Use safe YAML loading (priority: medium)
  - Replace `new Yaml().load(str)` with safe constructors:
    - For SnakeYAML 1.x: use `new Yaml(new SafeConstructor())` or `Yaml.safeLoad(...)` if available.
    - Explicitly disallow type tags that create arbitrary Java objects.
  - Document that YAML load APIs should only be used on trusted config files; treat external YAML as untrusted input.

- Audit command execution sites (priority: medium)
  - Review all call sites that call `CmdUtil.execute(...)` or other `ProcessBuilder` usage to ensure arguments are not constructed from untrusted input or are properly validated/escaped.
  - Prefer passing command+args as an array rather than `sh -c` string interpolation.

- Add static checks and CI policies (priority: medium)
  - Add a security-focused static analysis step to CI:
    - SpotBugs + security plugin, `spotbugs` or `errorprone`.
    - OWASP Dependency-Check or GitHub Dependabot to flag vulnerable dependencies (e.g., SnakeYAML versions).
    - A linter (rg checks) to fail builds on dangerous patterns (e.g., `ObjectInputStream` without filter, `HostnameVerifier` that returns true, `new Yaml().load(`).
  - Add a short SECURITY.md or developer docs describing safe usage patterns: how/when to disable TLS verification (and that it's only for testing), safe deserialization policy, YAML handling.

**Relevant files & lines (quick references)**

- Insecure TLS defaults:
  - `solon-projects/solon-net/solon-net-httputils/src/main/java/org/noear/solon/net/http/impl/HttpSsl.java` — `DefaultX509TrustManager`, `DefaultHostnameVerifier`, `getSSLSocketFactory()`.

## CWE-22 (Path Traversal / Zip Slip)

There is no exploitable CWE-22.  
CWE-22 (official intent): a pathname is built using external input for a file/dir that is supposed to stay under a restricted parent directory/allowed file set, but special path elements are not properly neutralized so the resolved path can escape the restriction.

Scope: Fail on either (A) app-exploitable path traversal in this repo’s real deployment or (B) artifact-exploitable: a shipped artifact exposes an exposed API surface that plausibly processes untrusted path or archive-entry input and performs OS filesystem I/O without robust containment (even if the repo itself doesn’t call it).

Attacker / trust model (precision-first):
- Attacker-controlled only if repo/docs support remote/low-privilege supply via production interfaces (requests, uploads, attacker-writable DB/queue, etc.).
- CLI/env/local config/admin-only consoles/test/dev endpoints/operator-only inputs are trusted unless docs say otherwise.
- For shipped artifacts, inputs to exposed API surface are attacker-controlled only if intended/plausible downstream use involves untrusted content (e.g., extract/unzip/import/resource/plugin handling), supported by docs/examples/naming/role.

What counts as a CWE-22 sink:
- Any runtime-reachable OS filesystem operation using the constructed/resolved path (in repo code or stdlib/deps): open/read/write/delete/list, temp files, move/copy/rename, and archive extraction writing entries to disk (Zip Slip).

This test FAILs only if ALL are true:
1) Surface: Either (A) a production-reachable attacker-controlled entry point exists, or (B) shipped exposed API surface plausibly takes untrusted path/archive-entry input and reaches a filesystem sink.
2) Dataflow: The attacker-controlled value (or derived value, including archive entry names) influences the path used at the sink.
